purpose: Saved post-cohort seven-row UI result used only as a semantic regression fixture, not a benchmark answer or model prompt.

plan.estimand: Difference in means between two independent normally distributed groups
plan.hypothesis: Two-sided test of equality of means: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ vs H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂
assumptions: Two independent groups with normal distributions
Common known standard deviation (Cohen d convention)
Pooled variance t-test with equal allocation (1:1)
Asymptotic normality of test statistic under alternative
scientific_notes: Cohen d = 0.5 represents a medium effect size
Using R stats::power.t.test() with strict=TRUE for exactness
Will report power at both the minimum integer n and n−1 per arm to demonstrate the threshold

answer.summary: For a two-sided pooled two-sample t-test comparing two independent normally distributed groups with Cohen d = 0.5, α = 0.05, and target power 0.80 under 1:1 equal allocation, the minimum integer sample size is **64 participants per arm (128 total participants)**. The exact continuous solution is 63.7656 per arm. At the minimum design (n = 64), achieved power is 0.8015, exceeding the 0.80 target. At n = 63, power is 0.7952, which falls below target, confirming that n = 64 is the smallest admissible integer design meeting the power requirement.
answer.method: Analytic inversion using R stats::power.t.test(strict=TRUE) for the pooled two-sample t-test. The method inverts from the target power condition to solve for n, using the noncentral t distribution with degrees of freedom ν = 2n − 2 and noncentrality parameter λ = δ√(n/2) = 0.5√(n/2). The continuous solution (63.7656) is then rounded up to the nearest integer (64) and verified by power re-computation at both n and n − 1.
assumptions: Two independent groups, each normally distributed with a common population standard deviation
Pooled-variance Student's t-test with test statistic t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/(sp√(2/n)), where sp is the pooled standard deviation
Two-sided hypothesis test (H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ vs H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂)
Cohen d = 0.5 effect size, representing a standardized mean difference
Under the alternative hypothesis, the test statistic follows a noncentral t distribution with ν = 2n − 2 degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter λ = δ√(n/2)
limitations: Assumes normality of the underlying populations; departures from normality (e.g., heavy tails, skew) may affect Type I and Type II error rates in finite samples
Assumes homogeneity of variance across the two groups; unequal variances would necessitate Welch's correction and alter the power calculation
Uses the asymptotic/exact noncentral t distribution; practical power may vary slightly with actual sample characteristics
Does not account for multiple testing, sequential analysis, or multiplicity adjustment
No inflation for attrition, loss to follow-up, or non-compliance; any such effects must be handled separately
Power is sensitive to the true effect size; if the population effect differs from Cohen d = 0.5, actual power will differ
